messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Asha Menon was a 50-year-old South Asian diplomat who had spent much of her adult life managing crises in other people’s countries, presenting a steady face in rooms where tension had to be contained. Her own crisis began on a work assignment that seemed, at first, routine: a government building where a chemical leak was reported after a storage tank malfunctioned. She remembered the sharp, bitter taste that flooded her mouth when she entered the corridor, the metallic sting coating her tongue before anyone had even fully understood what was happening. In the confusion that followed, several people became sick, alarms sounded, and she was hustled out through a side exit while wearing the same suit she had put on that morning. Months later, that taste could return with such force that it pulled the entire scene back into her body without warning. Sometimes it arrived in the middle of a meeting when someone mentioned maintenance in a building, sometimes while she was brushing her teeth, and when it came she would lose the thread of what she was saying, stopping mid-sentence with a blank, frustrated look as if the details had slipped past her on purpose. She found herself unable to explain the event clearly even to clinicians, circling around it, starting over, then shutting down.

Afterward, Asha began to avoid anything that could be stressful, which in her mind included news about industrial accidents, crowded committee rooms, and even the unfamiliar scent of cleaning products in office hallways. She told herself, in a quiet and increasingly practiced way, that what happened had not really happened, or at least not in the catastrophic way her body seemed to insist it had. That kind of thinking gave her temporary relief, and for a while she tried to carry on at work by pushing away any thoughts of the incident, refusing to let her mind linger on the corridor, the smell, or the taste. But the more she avoided thinking about it, the more vulnerable she became to being caught off guard by fragments of it. A whiff of solvent in the embassy basement, a comment about chemical safety in a briefing, even the glare of fluorescent lights in a conference center could make the memory break through all at once, vivid and bodily, as if it had been waiting just beneath the surface. Each unwanted return of the memory strengthened her resolve to keep distance from anything that might stir it again, and her world narrowed accordingly: she delegated site visits, declined invitations that involved unknown venues, and began arranging her days so that stress could be anticipated and sidestepped.

Yet this shrinking life did not bring her peace. Asha became constantly tense, ready to react to danger, and found herself scanning her surroundings for signs of threat in a way that was exhausting and hard to turn off. In public buildings she checked exits before she sat down; in restaurants she watched for unusual smells; at work she noticed ventilation systems, storage areas, and the faces of staff members longer than she once would have. She had always been composed, but now irritable behavior and angry outbursts surfaced with little warning, especially when colleagues interrupted her concentration or failed to understand why she needed to leave a room. She hated this change in herself. The tension in her body made her feel as though danger could arrive at any instant, and that constant readiness made the memory easier to catch and harder to dismiss. When her muscles were braced and her attention fixed on possible hazards, a smell or taste could abruptly snap her back to the exposure, and once the memory surged forward, she would become more keyed up, more suspicious, more certain that she had to protect herself from the next shock.

As the months passed, the relationship between her avoidance and her symptoms tightened. The more Asha tried to keep stress and reminders at bay, the more fragile she felt when reminders found her anyway. She stopped taking on the assignments she once enjoyed because the possibility of an unfamiliar building, an unfamiliar air system, or an unexpected smell seemed too risky. This protected her from immediate distress, but it also left her less able to test whether she could tolerate being near reminders without falling apart. At home she sat with her thoughts carefully diverted, reading the same reports twice because she could not stay with anything that might drift toward the event. The result was not calm but a kind of brittle vigilance. Her body remained on alert, her temper shortened, and the memory stayed potent precisely because it was never allowed to be spoken through from beginning to end. Even now, when she tries to describe what happened, she can manage the first few details before the taste in her mouth seems to return and the story breaks apart.

Asha sought help after one particularly difficult week at work, when a maintenance odor in the embassy made her so tense and angry that she snapped at a junior staff member and then had to leave the building. What frightened her most was not only that the memory still arrived so powerfully, but that her life was becoming organized around escaping anything that might bring it back. She hoped therapy might help her make sense of the event without losing the thread, and she was afraid that if she kept living this way, the world would keep shrinking around her until even ordinary places felt dangerous.
